A. Soriano Corporation (ANS) was incorporated on February 13, 1930, with various investments in companies engaged in a range of activities both local and abroad.

The Company's major investments are in Phelps Dodge Philippines Energy Products Corporation, which manufactures wire and cable products, and Seven Seas Resorts and Leisure, Inc., which owns and operates the Amanpulo Resort in Pamalican Island, Palawan. ANS also has other investments in companies engaged in a range of activities in the Philippines including aviation, business process outsourcing, and real estate.

ANS has several direct and indirect subsidiaries operating in various industries, including A. Soriano Air Corporation; Anscor Consolidated Corporation; Anscor International, Inc.; Anscor Holdings, Inc.; Sutton Place Holdings, Inc.; Summerside Corporation; Phelps Dodge International Philippines, Inc.; AFC Agribusiness Corporation; Seven Seas Resorts and Leisure, Inc.; Vicinetum Holdings, Inc.; Fremont Holdings, Inc.; TBG Food Holdings, Inc.; ATRAM Investment Management; and KSA Realty Corporation.

Source: SEC Form 17-A (2024)

storedThesis:
A. Soriano Corporation is a diversified holding company whose operating heartbeat is two very different but understandable businesses: Phelps Dodge Philippines, a wire and cable manufacturer serving the construction and energy sectors, and Seven Seas Resorts & Leisure, which owns and operates Amanpulo — the ultra-exclusive Aman-branded private island resort off Palawan. Rounding it out are ATRAM Investment Management, KSA Realty, a small aviation unit, and a large liquid investment portfolio. The conglomerate structure adds opacity, but the underlying businesses are not complicated. Amanpulo is a luxury hospitality asset charging ₱116,924 per room night as of Q1 2025 — you either get it or you don't. Phelps Dodge is a branded industrial manufacturer with international lineage. This clears the Meaning bar, if narrowly.

The moat question is where ANS gets genuinely interesting. Amanpulo is about as close to an irreplaceable asset as you'll find on PSE — a private island, a globally recognized Aman brand, and pricing power that has proven immune to volume softness (occupancy fell to 45.4% in 2024 yet revenue held up because rates climbed 14%). You cannot replicate that island, that brand, or that clientele. Phelps Dodge Philippines completed its first high-voltage submarine cable project in 2025 and posted a record ₱1 billion net income on ₱12.3 billion in sales — specialized manufacturing capability that isn't easily disrupted. The investment portfolio and ATRAM add compounding optionality. The moat is real but concentrated in two assets; the rest of the conglomerate is ordinary.

Management is the story of disciplined capital allocation with a leadership transition risk attached. The Bistro Group flip — ₱1.61B in November 2024, sold for ₱1.91B in October 2025 at 25%+ annualized returns — is a clean signal that the Soriano family knows how to buy, hold briefly, and exit. The iPeople sale to Ayala is further evidence of pruning non-core assets. The balance sheet is almost absurdly conservative: debt/equity of 0.02x and a net cash position of ₱25.46 billion against a market cap of roughly ₱19.22 billion. That last figure deserves emphasis — ANS has more cash than its entire stock market value, meaning investors are implicitly getting Amanpulo, Phelps Dodge, ATRAM, and everything else for negative consideration. The death of vice chairman Eduardo Soriano in February 2025 is a loss, but succession appears orderly — his son has joined the board, and chairman Andres "Andy" Soriano III remains the strategic anchor. No red flags in governance.

On valuation, the Rule #1 numbers tell a conflicted story. The sticker price (₱17.38) essentially equals today's price (₱17.26), which means you're at fair value — not at the 50% margin of safety that Phil Town demands. The MOS buy price is ₱8.69, and the current price sits 98.6% above that level. By the strict framework, this is not a buy. However, the traditional Rule #1 sticker price calculation may misprice this particular situation: when net cash alone exceeds market cap, the enterprise value of the operating businesses is *negative*, which fundamentally challenges whether ₱8.69 is even a coherent target. The ROIC of 17.8% sustained over a decade, 15.7% EPS growth, and 44.8% FCF growth are not the numbers of a value trap — they are exceptional for a Philippine conglomerate. The market's persistent willingness to assign a 30% discount to book value reflects the classic holding company penalty, not business deterioration.

The bottom line is a watch at the current price for a disciplined Rule #1 investor. You are paying fair value for genuinely excellent underlying businesses, conservative management, and a balance sheet that could withstand almost any macro shock. The margin of safety simply isn't there at ₱17.26 — you want meaningful downside protection, not precisely fair value. Watch for: a price retreat toward ₱12–13 range (still above MOS but offering a more reasonable entry), any announcement of how management intends to deploy the cash hoard (a large capital allocation decision could be a catalyst in either direction), and Amanpulo occupancy trends heading into the 2026 peak season. If the market gives you ₱12 on general PSE weakness, this becomes a serious buy.
